title: Single Number II
description: Brute force to optimized: a hash map versus per bit position modulo 3 counting versus a single pass bitmask state machine.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array nums where every element appears exactly three times except for one element which appears only once, find that single element.

blocks.caption: Every element repeats three times except one; count each bit modulo 3 to isolate it

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an integer array nums where every element appears exactly three times except for one element which appears only once, find that single element.

blocks.title: Analogy: The One Item Missing Its Usual Set of Three
blocks.text: Like a warehouse shelf where every item type is normally stocked in sets of exactly three identical units, except for one lone item that only has a single unit, and the task is to spot it.

blocks.caption: Every value appears exactly three times except one, which needs to be found

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [2, 2, 3, 2]

blocks.text: Edge case: a single element array
With only one element and nothing else to compare against, that element is trivially the answer.
5. How Should We Think?

This is the natural next step after the "everything paired, one exception" version of Single Number: here everything is tripled instead of paired, and that single change is enough to break the usual XOR trick completely.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: XOR cancels a value with itself an even number of times, since XOR-ing anything with itself twice returns to 0; but XOR-ing a value with itself three times just leaves the value unchanged, not canceled, so a plain XOR of the whole array does not isolate the single element here.

Observation 2: Looking at just one bit position across the whole array, every repeated value contributes either 3 set bits or 0 set bits at that position (3 identical copies of the same bit), so the total count of set bits at that position, taken modulo 3, is entirely determined by the single unique value's bit there.

Observation 3: If the total set-bit count at a position is a multiple of 3, the single value's bit there is 0; if the remainder is 1, its bit there is 1 (it can never be 2, since only one number contributes an "extra" unpaired bit).

Observation 4: Repeating this per-bit-position count across all 32 bits and assembling the results reconstructs the single value one bit at a time, all without ever forming a hash map.

Whenever XOR cancellation breaks because values repeat k times instead of twice, count each bit position's occurrences and reduce modulo k instead of relying on XOR's built-in cancel-in-pairs behavior.

This bit-by-bit modulo counting is the direct generalization of the twice-repeated version's XOR trick, and it is itself just the first of two techniques this problem teaches, since the per bit position counting can later be compressed even further into a single pass.
6. Brute Force Solution
Count every value's frequency using a hash map, then return the value whose count is exactly 1.
Step by step algorithm

items: Build a frequency count for every value in the array.
Return the value whose count equals 1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: counts.get(num, 0) + 1 / getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1 safely builds up each value's frequency without a separate existence check the first time a value is seen.
The second loop scans the completed frequency map rather than the original array, since a value's true final count is only known after every occurrence has been tallied.
Returning -1 as a fallback is unreachable under this problem's guarantee that exactly one value has count 1, but it keeps the function's return type well-defined in all three languages.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every value's true count is directly computed, so the one value appearing only once is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to count, one pass over the distinct values.
Space: O(n), for the frequency map in the worst case.

Limitation: plain XOR cancellation (which solves the twice-repeated version of this problem) does not directly apply here, since XORing a value with itself three times leaves the value unchanged rather than canceling it, so a different bit level trick is needed to reach O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force spends O(n) extra space on a frequency map purely to later ask one simple question: which value's count is not a multiple of 3? Answering that question does not actually require remembering every value's exact count, only remembering enough per bit position to know whether the running total there is currently 0, 1, or 2 modulo 3, information a handful of integers can track instead of an entire hash map. Looking at the array one bit position at a time, rather than one value at a time, replaces value-keyed counting with position-keyed counting, and a position's count only ever needs to be known modulo 3, a tiny, bounded amount of information, not a full integer counter.

Consider each of the 32 bit positions independently. Since every repeated value contributes a multiple of 3 to the total count of set bits at any given position, the remainder of that total count modulo 3 reveals exactly what the single unique value's bit is at that position (a remainder of 1 means it is set, a remainder of 0 means it is not). Building up the answer bit by bit this way reconstructs the single value directly.
9. Optimized Solution
For each bit position, count how many numbers have it set, and take that count modulo 3.
Dry run for nums = [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 99] (99 is binary 1100011)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bit position","Count of set bits","Count modulo 3","Answer bit","Why"],"rows":[["bit 0","3 (three 1s) plus 1 (from 99) = 4","4 mod 3 = 1","1","The three 1s each contribute a set bit at position 0, and 99 (ending in ...011) contributes one more, totaling 4, which leaves remainder 1"],["bit 1","3 (three 1s) plus 1 (from 99) = 4","4 mod 3 = 1","1","The same three 1s each contribute a set bit at position 1 too, plus 99 contributes one more, again totaling 4 with remainder 1"],["bit 5","1 (only from 99)","1 mod 3 = 1","1","Only 99 has bit 5 set; 0 and 1 never reach that high a bit, so the count is exactly 1, already the single value's own contribution"],["bit 6","1 (only from 99)","1 mod 3 = 1","1","Only 99 has bit 6 set, the same reasoning as bit 5"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: for each bit, the total set count modulo 3 reveals the single value's bit

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32 times n), 32 passes over the array, one per bit position.
Space: O(1) extra, only a counter per bit position is kept.
Why This Works

Since every repeated value contributes its bit at a given position exactly 3 times (all 3 copies share the same bit pattern), the repeated values always add a multiple of 3 to that position's total set-bit count. Only the single unique value can break that multiple-of-3 pattern, contributing either 0 or 1 extra, so the remainder after dividing by 3 exactly recovers the single value's own bit at that position, with no other information needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Total set-bit count mod 3","Single value's bit at this position"],"rows":[["0","0 (the single value does not have this bit set)"],["1","1 (the single value has this bit set)"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The outer loop runs bit from 0 to 31, one iteration per bit position in a 32-bit integer.
(num >> bit) & 1 isolates exactly one bit of num, shifting the bit of interest down to position 0 and masking away everything else.

count % 3 == 1 checks the remainder directly rather than checking count == 1 or count == 4, since the actual total can be any multiple of 3 plus 0 or 1 depending on how many values happen to be in the array.

The final answer >= 2**31 check (Python only) converts the accumulated bit pattern back into a signed 32-bit integer, since Python has no fixed-width integer overflow the way Java and C++ do natively.

blocks.text: 10. Further Optimization: Single Pass Bitmask State Machine

The 32 pass approach can be replaced by a single pass over the array using two accumulator bitmasks that together track, for each bit position, how many times (modulo 3) that bit has been seen so far, cycling through the states 0, 1, and 2 as each new number is processed. This achieves the same result in one pass over the array instead of 32 separate passes, a genuine reduction in total work even though the asymptotic time complexity class stays the same.
Dry run for the state transitions on a single bit position, processing three 1s in a row

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","ones accumulator bit","twos accumulator bit","Meaning"],"rows":[["Start","0","0","seen 0 times so far"],["After first 1","1","0","seen 1 time so far"],["After second 1","0","1","seen 2 times so far"],["After third 1","0","0","seen 3 times so far, cycled back to 0"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: two accumulator bitmasks track each bit's count modulo 3 in a single pass

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over the array.
Space: O(1), only the two accumulator bitmasks are kept.
Code walkthrough

items: ones and twos each start at 0 and together encode, per bit position, whether that bit has been seen 0 times (both 0), 1 time (ones bit set), or 2 times (twos bit set) modulo 3, cycling back to 0 on the third occurrence.

ones = (ones ^ num) & ~twos updates ones for every bit of num, but only for bits that are not currently marked as "seen twice" in twos, which is what keeps the cycle from advancing past state 2 incorrectly.

twos = (twos ^ num) & ~ones runs the same kind of update for twos, using the already-updated ones to decide which bits are eligible, so the two accumulators always transition together through the correct 0 to 1 to 2 to 0 cycle.

After the full pass, ones holds exactly the bits seen a number of times congruent to 1 modulo 3, which is exactly the single value's own bit pattern, so ones is returned directly with no further per-bit reconstruction needed.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

This problem generalizes single number cancellation from "everything paired, one exception" to "everything tripled, one exception", and its further round shows how a per bit position modulo counting idea can be compressed into a single pass state machine using just two bitmasks, a technique that itself generalizes further to "every value appears k times except one" for other values of k.
Common mistakes

items: Trying to apply plain XOR cancellation directly: XOR-ing a value with itself three times leaves it unchanged rather than canceling it, so the twice-repeated version's trick simply does not transfer here.

Getting the ones and twos update order backwards in the single pass state machine: since twos's update depends on the already-updated ones, computing them in the wrong order breaks the intended 0 to 1 to 2 to 0 cycling.

Checking count == 1 instead of count % 3 == 1 in the per-bit approach: the actual total set-bit count at a position can be any multiple of 3 plus 0 or 1, not just exactly 0 or 1, once the array has more than a handful of elements.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Present the 32 pass modulo counting approach first, since its reasoning is easier to explain clearly, then offer the two bitmask state machine as a further refinement once the core idea is understood.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Every element appears k times except one," for a k other than 2, signals that plain XOR cancellation will not work directly, pointing toward per-bit-position counting modulo k, and potentially a further bitmask state machine refinement.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this generalize to every element appearing k times except one, for an arbitrary k? The same per-bit modulo-k counting works directly; the two-accumulator state machine generalizes to more accumulators (enough to represent counts 0 through k minus 1) but grows more intricate to implement correctly.

What if there could be two different single-appearing values instead of one? A different technique is needed, since a single 32-pass modulo-3 count would blend both values' bits together; separating them typically needs an extra partitioning step based on a bit where the two values differ.

Can the single pass state machine be derived without seeing it in advance? Yes, by starting from the per bit position modulo 3 counting insight and asking how to track a 0/1/2 cycle using bitwise operations instead of an explicit counter per bit.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Direct generalization of the classic Single Number problem (values paired, one exception) to values tripled, one exception.
Same "reduce a per-bit count modulo something" idea as Total Hamming Distance, though there the modulo was implicit through multiplication rather than an explicit remainder.

The two-accumulator bitmask state machine is a small instance of the broader finite-state-machine-via-bitwise-operations technique, also seen in problems tracking a handful of possible states per bit or per element without any extra data structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (per bit position modulo 3 counting): O(32 times n) time, O(1) space.
Further optimized (bitmask state machine): O(n) time, O(1) space, in a single pass.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Per-bit-position modulo-k counting (here k = 3) to isolate a single non-repeating value
Core Idea: A value repeated exactly 3 times contributes a multiple of 3 to each bit position's total set-bit count, so the remainder modulo 3 reveals the single value's bits directly
Time: O(n) for both the modulo-3 counting version (with a fixed 32x factor) and the single-pass bitmask state machine
Space: O(1) extra for both optimized approaches, O(n) for the brute force

Most Important Observation: XOR cancellation only works for pairs; a repeat count of 3 needs modulo-3 reasoning instead, whether done per bit position across 32 passes or compressed into a single pass with two accumulator bitmasks
Interview Difficulty: Medium to Hard
One-line memory trick: Tripled values vanish mod 3, the lone value is the remainder
